changes.before: Register two, the ground of truth: on what are judgments about avowal, value and relations true. Here the series has no complete position, and this essay does not acquire one for it. Note that a value-content's being constituted by a subject and there being an objective ground of truth for judgments about it are two things. Even with content coming by constitution, the following can still be objective facts: whether he ever completed that avowal; whether that content still has standing now; whether the channel of revision has been sealed; whether some external attribution is counterfeiting constitution. So subject-dependence in constitution is not anti-realism about truth. Metaethics itself disputes whether constructivism counts as realism and whether objectivity requires mind-independence; this series does not settle that whole layer in one stroke from constitutive dependence.

changes.before: One more thing to keep apart, and Kant scholarship argues about it too: respecting another's humanity and approving every end he chooses are not one thing. Dean folds a morally good will into the core of humanity; the criticism replies that even where a man's particular choice is evil, the capacity to choose must still be respected. On the value-theory side, the three limits say which operations I do not have on another's values — reading cannot close into a reading guaranteed complete, value-standings take no common external ruler, relational facts do not merge existing sources. changes.before: The family's own famous difficulty comes from the same place: the wrong kind of reasons. A demon can threaten to punish you unless you admire something worthless; you then really do have a prudential reason to admire it, and that reason seems not to make it admirable in the least. So the problem is not finding a reason but separating, non-circularly, reasons given by the object from reasons given by the consequences of the attitude. Rabinowicz and Rønnow-Rasmussen, and Olson among others, have treated the difficulty specifically. If in the end the right kind of reason can only be defined as the kind that reflects the object's value, the direction of explaining value by reasons has circled back. This essay does not judge whether the difficulty succeeds; it points out that it lies at the same place as the disagreement.

changes.before: It is tempting to cite Against Music and Moderation in Funerals as showing the Mohists judging some people's cherished rites as improper by the benefit of all under heaven, and so reaching into the side where value holds. The texts themselves do not take that step. Against Music explicitly grants that the ear knows music as pleasing, the eye knows ornament as beautiful, the mouth knows fine food as sweet — and only then, because the great lords have instruments made, levy taxes and consume labour, judges it as not according with the affairs of the sage kings above and not according with the benefit of the myriad people below. Moderation in Funerals likewise tests lavish burial and long mourning, as an institutionalized practice, against wealth, population and order. So what the Mohists judge is music-making and lavish burial as public practice, governance and allocation of resources — not a proof that what is cherished is not worth cherishing. Against Music even contains a line that reads almost as a pre-emptive exclusion of that misreading.

changes.before: Value pluralism and incommensurability. Three words apart: incommensurable means lacking a common unit of measure; incomparable means no comparison relation holds between two items; the first does not entail the second. Chang proposes a fourth relation — parity — where two items under an evaluative covering are neither better, nor worse, nor equal, and still within one evaluative space. This series' position here goes only so far: it holds definitely that value-standings take no common external ruler and rejects the predicates better, worse and equal. Whether it further holds incomparability, or allows some non-metric relation, the object-level text has not judged. And the fact that the world's conditions and consequences can be jointly checked cannot settle it: objects on the world side entering joint evaluation says nothing about a positive comparison relation between two value-standings.
changes.after: Value pluralism and incommensurability. Three words apart: incommensurable means lacking a common unit of measure; incomparable means no comparison relation holds between two items; the first does not entail the second. Chang proposes a fourth relation — parity — where two items under an evaluative covering are neither better, nor worse, nor equal, and still within one evaluative space. This series' position here goes only so far: it holds definitely that value-standings take no common external ruler and rejects the predicates higher, lower and equal. Whether it further holds incomparability, or allows a non-metric relation such as parity, the object-level text has not judged. And the fact that the world's conditions and consequences can be jointly checked cannot settle it: objects on the world side entering joint evaluation says nothing about a positive comparison relation between two value-standings.
changes.reason: Restore the rank predicates and the explicit example of the undecided non-metric relation.

changes.before: Preference, utility, welfare in economics — the three equals signs come off, as above; price was already routed out by the prequel, and preference, utility and welfare still have to be placed separately: their relation to end-value standing cannot be settled by price's routing. The place that really meets is Sen, taken up above. Harsanyi's theorem: under expected-utility axioms and certain consistency conditions, social evaluation has a weighted-sum representation. That does not prove a natural utility yardstick exists; it proves that under explicit normative and representational conditions, aggregation can have a strict structure. And what it does not solve must be said: it does not itself answer which welfare information is interpersonally comparable, where the weights come from, or what the normative ground is. This series does not oppose the theorem, so the two are not opposed.

changes.before: Slot one — the remainder this construct left: whether another bearer can hold separately. The people by the river dredged it, stopped the sand-mining, repaired the embankment. What was judged is that those undertakings do not entail their sources having merged, because each source is anchored in him and crossing pointings is not merging. What was not judged — and expressly so — is whether another bearer can hold under other conditions; and even if one could, that would not mean the original people's sources were swallowed by it. That is an express reservation and also a remainder. All this series' source-position, constitutive and running predicates take an already-holding bearer as their subject. The domain of bearers gives who can bear end-value, not how a new bearer comes about; the type-transition from several subjects or a relational structure to a new bearer has no corresponding occurrence-predicate in the seven essays. And this is not an accidentally omitted criterion: it exposes that the machine's input types lack a transition mechanism. Force the existing predicates onto that transition and you must first make the not-yet-holding bearer the subject of those predicates, and the argument is circular. That failure to absorb, caused by the input types themselves, is why it is listed as a remainder. Two things do not follow: it does not mean a third person cannot describe the conditions of a new bearer's formation — describing conditions and performing constitution are two things, and the second bar forbids only the latter; and it does not prejudge whether a relation can be a cause or condition in some such holding, which was expressly left unjudged.

changes.before: Slot two — objects adjacent in jurisdiction, never raised as questions. Two of them. Institutions. The sixth essay wrote that things done together, rules made together, things kept together are not wrong by virtue of being common, and gave a condition for when a common content becomes an external ruler. That is a condition for judging whether it oversteps, not an account of what an institution is; the series never raised that as its own question, and even mentioning it was incidental. Incidentally shown and never raised is not the same as expressly unjudged: the former was never even asked, so it is not a reservation and not a remainder — it is an adjacent object. Whoever takes it up should take up not how are institutions possible in that width, but the segment this series showed: under what conditions do common rules, common decisions and common arrangements acquire institutional structure. Fraser's side, tying misrecognition to institutionalized cultural value patterns, is the nearest ready material — that says where material is, not who the question is handed to. The cross-subject informational basis of public evaluation. Sen showed the other, and it is far wider than a single quantity: what welfare, utility, capability, resources, health, opportunity and consequences each have as subjects; which can be jointly checked; which can form partial comparisons or public orderings; why they do not thereby flow back into personal value-standing; and where the force comes from when a public evaluation acquires force in action or institutions. Also an adjacent object, not a remainder. And its destination is deliberately not written — writing a destination is opening a debt, and this essay opens none.
